To see how difficult it would be, I wrote a WASM-based polyfill that attempts to allow existing code to continue functioning, while not using native XSLT features from the browser. The polyfill is located on GitHub or as an npm package:

- https://github.com/mfreed7/xslt_polyfill 
- https://www.npmjs.com/package/xslt-polyfill

This contains a functional polyfilled replacement for the XSLTProcessor class, plus a utility function for an easy way to replace XML documents that use XSLT processing instructions. Of course, XSLT would also continue to be executable on the server side if needed.

In addition, site count may not reflect actual human beings impacted directly. The Stratford Library Association (fifth most popular site triggering XSLProcessingInstruction according to [Chrome Platform Status](https://chromestatus.com/metrics/feature/timeline/popularity/78) right now) has 46,000+ clients according to their own numbers.

I vaguely remember the mood twenty-something years ago among several browser vendors and Web/XML nerds was that XSL(T) _should not_ be used or even be available client-side in the first place. (Some said the same about SVG back then, though.)

However, some company saw a business opportunity in shipping it anyway, then some adoption by authors followed, expectations build up and other vendors felt the need to also add it. Nobody ever loved XSLT for its syntax, but for its features. However, market penetration and demand apparently never pushed anyone to adopt subsequent editions in general-purpose browsers. Such stagnation is usually a sign that everybody already considers it dead anyway. Maybe it is about time to declare it thus indeed.

Or rather of the fact that in the meantime the web got so centralized that the only “innovation” that gets adoption is what GAFAM decides (see e.g. their repeated attempts to suppress RSS, the attempt to kill SMIL in 2015 —with arguments similar to the ones that are being made today for XSLT today— or the aborted adoption of JPEG XL; how's that MathML support going on in Chrome BTW?) rather than what's needed for the open web to flourish.

The use case is that it's already being used, on websites built once and not actively maintained (albeit still updated with content). A polyfill users have to deploy themselves is not a solution.

Fully understand the rationale. The usage stats speak for themselves, and the security concerns are real. No disagreement there.

That said, echoing @daveajones above, there is a real-world and modern use case from the podcasting industry, where I work. Collectively, we [host over 4.5 million RSS feeds](https://podcastindex.org/stats). Like many other podcast hosting companies, we use XSLT to beautify our raw feeds and make them easier to understand when viewed in a browser.

This is not about nostalgia or legacy tech. Podcast feeds are still actively distributed and submitted by creators around the world often by copy-pasting their RSS feed URL. When they open that URL in a browser and see raw XML, it creates friction. But with XSLT, we can show them something visual: cover art, episode titles, and descriptions, instead of what looks to them like unreadable "code".

RSS feeds remain one of the last open and decentralized distribution mechanisms on the modern web. Platforms like Spotify and YouTube are increasingly moving toward exclusivity and closed podcasting ecosystems. Supporting browser-side XSLT helps keep RSS accessible and human-friendly, especially for independent creators. This ties in directly with the ethos of openness that underpins the web itself, and also the work of groups like WHATWG.

I just wanted to make sure this current, real, and widely deployed use case is part of the broader conversation. In our case, XSLT is mainly used to add a visual skin to RSS feeds. Given the legitimate security concerns, perhaps we could consider some new form of minimal, aesthetic-only XSLT-like functionality, e.g. a declarative visual layer for XML, stripped of all the logic that makes XSLT insecure, and supported by a lightweight library. This could open the door to deprecating libraries like libxslt while still preserving the spirit and utility of this visual enhancement for open data formats.

Something that was pointed out is that serving html to the feed.xml request (to use the polyfill) won't work because some RSS feed viewers also support parsing HTML (so will send text/html in their accept header). Something to think about wrt how we can enable deployment of the polyfill to meet this use case.

On the other side of things I've also been looking and some of the example feeds that have been linked to me already don't render correctly in Firefox due to Firefox's differing implementation, now yes it can be said that firefox should update but they're not a market dominator and that's engineering time that can and imo should be spent elsewhere. Something that's not interopable (apparently the standard even marks this particular part of xslt as optional which isn't very good for a "web standard") doesn't feel like a good fit for the modern web platform. So if we can address the use cases in another (potentially better) way then that seems worthwhile investigating.

To explore further, I looked at the top-10 podcasts (from [this list](https://rss.com/blog/popular-rss-feeds/)) and did some digging. Raw data is [here](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/11guip4ZzZQHxE2FdsF95Lcdc1VzOZHFncbEWm10cG_w). Here's what I found in those podcasts:

- 5 out of 10 use a `<link rel="alternate" type="application/rss+xml">` on their (html-based) website to allow RSS readers to pick up the RSS link.

I'm not sure what to make of these data. Perhaps these are the largest podcasts, so they feel less pressure to help their users find the feed or deal with accidental navigations to the RSS feed itself?

The use case of transforming RSS/Atom feeds, of podcasts in particular, client-side into simple HTML+CSS for nicer display in browsers *could* almost always be solved by CSS in XML, ` `, *if* CSS Generated Content was just a bit more powerful, e.g. enabled authors to pull in (child) element content similar to `attr()` and handling hyperlinks. ~~~~ css * { display: none; } rss, channel, item, title { display: block; } description, image { display: inline-block; /* grid, flex, whatever */ } image { content: attr(url type()) / string(--caption); /* restriction lifted */ } image::link /* new pseudo-element */ { content: string(--destination type() /* extended capability */ local) / attr(url type()); } image > link { string-set: --destination contents; } image > title { string-set: --caption contents; } ~~~~

We run a website with millions of custom RSS feeds, accessible via the interface at https://www.fixmystreet.com/alert
The service lets you sign up for a particular location or area by email or get an RSS feed, and being able to style the RSS feed via XSLT means it all works smoothly. We point people at the feed directly, as that is then easy for people to copy either from the page shown or from the URL bar; we have a wide user base, and we don't expect people to take the results page of a form and copy that into their RSS feed reader without guidance. This has run well for nearly 20 years now.

I haven't used XSLT in browsers much since the early 2000s, since then only using it to style RSS & ATOM feeds. The reason I stopped using it is because of being stuck with XSLT v1.0.

Rather than removal, would advancing the engine to XSLT v3.0 be feasible? There will be some backward compatibility breaks, but fewer than if it was removed entirely.

> No, the polyfill would need to be incorporated into the site - it wouldn't be part of the browser.

This would introduce a so-far unnecessary dependency on JavaScript for websites that have managed to stay JS-free.

> Rather than removal, would advancing the engine to XSLT v3.0 be feasible? There will be some backward compatibility breaks, but fewer than if it was removed entirely.

Seconded. Advancing to XSLT 3 and adopting a more secure library addresses the issues without breaking the web, especially the more open, independent part of the web.

I support removing XSLT. Being stuck on XSLT v1, and with an aging codebase with little attention paid to it, is not a good situation to be in.

I suspect the vast majority of XSLT usage today is indeed just formatting RSS feeds. We already have alternate solutions for that - just serving HTML for the human-readable version, with a `<link>` pointing to the XML file, works in every RSS tool. It's relatively trivial to generate that on the server at the same time as you generate the RSS file, and it avoids any need for JS.

I don't think there's a strong "Open Web" argument to be made here. XML data files being able to be reformatted into HTML is somewhat of an accident of history; we don't have similar functionality for *any other data type*, despite, for example, JSON files being *vastly* more common on the web than XML.

@tabatkins It seems there are two assumptions here that I don't share. If nothing else, I'll learn something new, please clarify or correct me.

1. Websites use RSS as human-readable index instead of having an HTML web page.

It sounds like you think this is central to XSLT usage today. If yes, can you share examples? I've not encountered websites that serve RSS feeds as their website index, instead of having an HTML web page. Nor have I heard of people adopting XSLT out of concern that someone might curiously (or mistakenly) copy a feed URL from view-source or from elsewhere and navigate to it from a new browser tab. Afaik that's not why https://aboutfeeds.com/ came about or why people adopt it.

2. Websites do not visibly link to their feed.

Feeds are often linked from visible anchor links. That's `<a>` with a text label or image, not `<link>`.  This includes our respective blogs at https://timotijhof.net/ and https://tabatkins.com/blog/, and WordPress sidebars/footers by default. A common frustration among feed users is actually that web authors _don't_ add a machine-discovery `<link>` (not knowing or forgetting).

In the early 2000s browsers had built-in feed aggregators (Firefox, Safari, and IE) along with native rich-text accessible RSS previews shown when navigating to an RSS/Atom resource (akin to PDF, JSON, and video viewers in browsers today). Now browsers have neither. The [feed scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feed_URI_scheme) hasn't taken off. I suspect in part due to anchor links having no way to render fallback "content", or a fallback "destination", for unhandled protocols. Mastodon `web+follow` and `share` suffer a similar flaw, making them unappealing to adopt without progressive enhancement. Ref https://github.com/WICG/proposals/issues/11, [Thoughts on Web Follow](https://paul.kinlan.me/thoughts-on-web-follow/).

Thus... it is natural today for feeds to end up in people's faces, by merely browsing a normal HTML web page and following a normal link. The obvious thing to do with a link, is to click it.

These stylesheets enable _in-situ_ discovery of the open web and feed readers. People familiar with feed readers open a website's homepage directly in a feed reader, and auto-discover the feed from an HTML `<link>`. However, that's a workflow one doesn't just stumble into. We lack a path from a visible anchor link for an RSS file, to having a feed reader setup and opening it there. XSLT provides that path today in a way that's easy for websites to adopt. What alternative should we invest in instead?

I think there's a reasonable argument to be made that XSLT isn't good _enough_, and that we need something _even_ easier to mass adopt. However, I'd like to make sure we make that argument explicitly, based on how and why this is used today.

> we don't have similar functionality for *any other data type*, despite, for example, JSON files being vastly more common on the web than XML.

Clearly that means we need to rip out the existing functionality for the sake of feature parity, and isn't an indicator that it might actually be nice to add it to other formats.

Not that I'm seriously advocating for stylesheets/translation for JSON, but I could make the same arguments about why do browsers only parse and render HTML but no built-in support for any other markup format like markdown?  (Which in absolute numbers is written by vastly more people than HTML to author text published online)  Clearly browsers should remove the massive security hole of tag soup parsing.

At $DAYJOB, we use XSLT in several places; we produce embedded equipment which is fairly busy doing whatever they are doing and outputting that information through an API as XML (most of this was written before JSON became a big thing). Instead of having additional code running on these platforms to also output the same information as HTML, we use XSLT to allow the API documents to be directly displayed in a browser. This approach has worked fine for the last two decades, and it would be a shame to lose it. Yes, you could probably write scripting to do it, but then you need to make space for that extra scripting in the device firmware, and you would need to make sure everyone using the devices upgrade to a newer release.

These are commercial devices not meant to be reachable from the wider internet, so they will usually not show up in any usage statistics, but they are very real.

This is not to say that doing such updates are impossible. We used some Adobe Flash components for graphing previously, which we replaced with canvas in 2016. We used still to get the odd question about this from customers still running older devices that have not yet been updated until just a few years ago.

XML being transformable into HTML and integrable into the wider web is not an “accident” of history, it was a specific aim of the standard when it was designed, and remains a worthwhile one despite the JavaScript brainworm that has destroyed the minds of the new generation (and has reached peaks such as proposal to deprecate HTML altogether in favor of doing everything via JS because “that what everybody does anyway”). The whole point of XML‌ as a language was to make everything easier to integrate. This is just one of the reasons why removing XSLT goes against the open web.

If we want to make it easier for JSON to be rendered directly, let's focus on designing a way to do that, which can be done without removing XSLT support from the browsers —in fact, the easiest way to achieve this is to define a canonical XML equivalent of the JSON *and then use XSLT to style it*.

For statically generated websites, requiring an HTML representation of every RSS or Atom feed means increasing *all* costs (generation, hosting, bandwidth), for something that is already doable much more efficiently with only the XML feed and an XSLT. This is just one on the many ways in which removing XSLT support (instead of improving on it) is against the indie web.

I have been using XSLT since it was in beta and the only browser that implemented it was MSIE 5.5. I designed and implemented an internationalized content pipeline using XSLT and DocBook at the job I had from 2002-2005. Since about 2007 I've been using XSLT regularly on the client side to transform (X)HTML into itself (as well as SVG and Atom), because it excels at bolting presentation markup onto plain semantic markup, and thus makes for an _extremely_ lazy templating language that exists separately from the JavaScript ecosystem. I use it on [my own](https://doriantaylor.com/) [Web properties](https://the.natureof.software/), and I use it on projects (I mainly do intranets). I have made libraries for [seamless transclusion](https://github.com/doriantaylor/xslt-transclusion) and [querying RDFa](https://github.com/doriantaylor/xslt-rdfa), and I use those on projects (like [Sense Atlas](https://senseatlas.net/), a nascent knowledge graph product I'm working on, and [Intertwingler](https://intertwingler.net/), the application server that powers it).

Why I still use XSLT:

* it's a standard
* it's fast (at least nominally)
* it's declarative
* it's orthogonal to JS
* it can mix any number of back-ends (because it's a standard and operates over standard inputs; I regularly use it to mix static and dynamic resources on the same page)
* it can only operate over information _you_ give it (modulo zero-days, apparently)
* it operates over _wholes_, i.e., it doesn't stitch together markup as text but rather operates over intact DOM structures.

The first and last points are probably the biggest reasons I still use it, and I suppose the latter may need some unpacking. An XSLT stylesheet is a well-formed XML document and only operates over well-formed XML documents, and (unless you put in the effort) is only capable of _producing_ well-formed (X|HT)ML documents. So you have a validity check baked in at a very low level. Every other templating language I've seen, going all the way back to server-side includes ([with one esoteric exception](http://clearsilver.net/)), seems to not be shy about chopping up the syntax of the target language.

I anticipate the knee-jerk reaction to this is "so what?". Why should you care whether your template language breaks the syntax of the target? The tooling can compensate and it's intact when you render it. I mean, I _guess_? But then you need more tooling when otherwise an off-the-shelf validator would do. But that I think is not even the main differentiator.

The key difference, and why I've stuck with XSLT for almost 25 years, is _cognitive_. When I make a hypermedia resource (I am deliberately not using the word "page"), I think about it as a discrete, atomic whole. I can consider that object (and the server-side code that generates it) in isolation. It loads in the browser and is well-formed and intact and navigable. _Then_ I can think about applying transformations to that object, and/or composing related objects together, as a separate act. When I write an XSLT template, I think about it like a function (in the mathematical sense) rather than a procedure. I see my job as not to stitch together fragments of markup but to describe the node tree that results from an input tree. When I look at so-called "modern" frameworks, I (still) don't see any of that.

The reason why the implementations are riddled with CVEs, in my opinion, is because of neglect. I am old enough to remember when HTML5 was competing with XHTML2✱ as the proposed next-generation HTML standard. It turned out that the pedantry of the XML parser was not only reviled by developers (and remains a source of confusion for users if they hit a bad patch of it), for markup it was actually unnecessary. Tastes changed, and people moved on. The browser vendors keep the parsers around, but they demonstrably put as little effort into them as they can get away with. (The biggest shortcomings of XSLT 1.0 were fixed in 2.0—in 2007—but of course the browsers never implemented it.)

> ✱ XHTML2 actually had some really good ideas (like transclude all the things), but its mission (something like "how do we make the best XML-based hypertext markup language") was ultimately wrong-headed. I am _also_ old enough to remember, however, that one of the central arguments for HTML5 (now just "HTML", of course) was not breaking backward-compatibility.

My proposal, then, is not to scrap XSLT, but to _rehabilitate_ it. When it first shipped, XSLT was a solid, open-standard solution to the bog-standard problem of generating presentation markup. How many times has the wheel of Web templating been reinvented for this framework or that? Where is the Open Web successor to XSLT? How about…_XSLT_?

At its core, XSLT is terrifically powerful, especially [its latest incarnation](https://www.w3.org/TR/xslt-30/) (which, incidentally, [can operate over JSON](https://www.w3.org/TR/xslt-30/#json)). There are, of course, challenges:

1. I would say problem number one is the syntax. XSLT is an extremely bulky, chatty language. Without syntax completion in your code editor you'd never get anything done. _But_, there are precedents for ameliorating this, like [the compact syntax for RelaxNG](https://relaxng.org/compact-tutorial-20030326.html), or the [Turtle](https://www.w3.org/TR/turtle/) or [JSON-LD](https://www.w3.org/TR/json-ld11/) syntaxes for RDF.
2. XSLT only operates over XML (except of course for 3.0 which made an accommodation for JSON). Well that's simple, bump XSLT to 3.1 and spec out how it should operate over HTML DOMs (case-insensitive tags, whatever), as well as an invocation hook analogous to the XSLT processing instruction.
3. Namespaces: Apparently people hate them? This is something I have never understood (because if you don't use namespaces you just end up reinventing them badly), but whatever, fine. You won't need namespaces in your XPath anyway if you're just transforming HTML.
4. XPath: I would actually put money on the likelihood that CSS selector semantics can embed fully into XPath, especially given that XPath 3.1 itself is extensible (worst case scenario is you cheat and just make a `css` function).
5. Debugging: currently sucks. This I would chalk up to the same neglect as the CVEs.

It would be eminently feasible to make a "**SWeT**", _Standard Web Templates_:

* easy, neat, declarative syntax, comparable to Sass or RNC ([I sketched one out in like 2019](https://doriantaylor.com/file/xslt-mockup))
* isomorphic (or at least injective onto) XSLT 3.0 (3.1?); compiles to it
* wouldn't have to touch namespaces or even XPath if you didn't want to (use CSS selectors instead)
* still capable of existing outside of the JS ecosystem, but can be accessed from JS/DOM just like XSLT 1.0 can

Now I can imagine somebody saying well I can go off and do that anyway; [there's a reference implementation](https://www.saxonica.com/saxonjs/index.xml) of XSLT 3.0 I can compile against (written, actually, by the spec's author), etc etc. I think that kind of misses the point of having a _standard_ templating language that you can rely on being baked into every Web browser. At least, I suppose, until they rip it out.

So I guess my ultimate question is, is there truly no appetite for a standard language for transforming markup, a thing we all have to do, on every project, all the time? A thing that for lack of a standard, locks us into this or that framework, or stymies [casual system heterogeneity](https://doriantaylor.com/intelligent-heterogeneity)? A thing that would make it _even easier_ to build the Web? Seems like a sensible idea, doesn't it?

Thanks for all of the comments, details, and information on this issue. It's clear that XSLT (and talk of removing it) strikes a nerve with some folks. I've learned a lot from the posts here.

I want to address one thing up-front. The reason for this issue, and this discussion, is because the XSLT that is shipped in browsers today is **a)** very old, **b)** not well maintained across browsers, **c)** barely used by websites today, and **d)** a serious security risk to *all* users, not just those that actively use XSLT. 

So while we (the Chrome team) do understand the posts suggesting a renewal and improvement instead of a removal, we are strongly convinced that this would not be the right way to spend our limited resources. Doing so would reduce our ability to work on other platform features where there is measurable developer impact and interest, and which drive the web forward. One example set of such things is [Interop 2025](https://web.dev/blog/interop-2025). Most of the features in Interop 2025 have widespread developer interest, and many of them **already** have much higher usage than XSLT, despite some being relatively new to the platform. This technology (XSLT) is simply one that didn’t stand the test of time **for client side usage in web browsers**. That does not take away from the technology itself.

To that end, I would like to focus this discussion on the use cases that do currently strongly rely on XSLT, and what viable alternatives can we find for them. Here are the specific use cases I've seen described in comments on this issue:

1. **RSS and Atom Feeds**: XSLT is used to make raw RSS and Atom feeds human-readable when viewed directly in a browser. The use case is that a user accidentally clicks on a site’s RSS feed link, rather than pasting that link into their RSS reader, and gets XML rather than something they can read.

    ➡ A proposal for this use case is to add `<link rel="alternate" type="application/rss+xml">` to the (HTML-based) site, rather than an explicit (user-visible) `<a href=”something.xml”>` that users might accidentally click. This solution allows RSS readers to find the feed if a user pastes in just the website URL, but it also allows human users to see regular HTML content. This also follows the normal web paradigm that HTML is for humans and XML is for machines. Of course this doesn’t solve the case where a user just “has” an RSS link from somewhere, and they paste it into their web browser (rather than their RSS reader).

2. **API Output for Embedded Devices**: Some commercial embedded devices use XSLT to transform XML API output into a human-readable HTML format, allowing the API to be directly viewed in a browser without needing additional code on the device or in the browser.

    ➡ This is an interesting use case. Since this is a very application specific use case, the shape of the solution might vary. But one potential lightweight solution would be to use a browser extension that simply automatically injects the XSLT polyfill into raw XML documents. That wouldn’t require any embedded device firmware changes at all, since the same feed would continue to work. I have just such an extension in progress right now, and I can share it when it gets published.

3. **Lazy Templating/Web Properties**: Web developers use XSLT on the client side to apply presentation markup to semantic markup, functioning as a lazy templating language that is separate from the JavaScript ecosystem.

    ➡ There are two “solutions” to this more general problem. For an existing site built in this way, I think that the easiest solution is likely just to add the [polyfill](https://github.com/mfreed7/xslt_polyfill) to maintain existing functionality. Or perform the XSLT transformation on the server side, and serve the resulting HTML to the client. The more long-term solution would be to migrate to a more modern JS/JSON-based framework.

-----

One last comment: it’s important to point out that this issue is just about XSLT, and there is no suggestion that we should remove XML itself from the browser. I just want to make that clear.

At one time many browsers had a native RSS "bug" that appeared at the address bar, however that is no longer the case in any browser, at least not without the use of an extension. The use of the `<link rel=` element is already quite common in RSS-using websites as it is considered ground-level requirements for auto-discovery of feeds by users with readers and experience using them. 

However, increasingly, there is a push by large companies to enclose RSS, especially for podcast, within specialized readers. This pushes websites to implement experiences that the user recognizes, a link to Feedly, a link to Spotify, a link to Apple Podcasts, etc... because the user understands that they click on that button and get access to a usable version of the feed. 

A link to an RSS feed without browser-native rendering is alien in this context. The link needs to be provided along-side these other feed-reading-systems, but without XSLT it cannot possibly compare in usability. It becomes harder to promote the idea of independent feed readers or podcast-catchers. It becomes harder to resist the enclosure of one of the web's few native open social technologies when you place a link to "subscribe to the RSS feed" on the page and that link leads to raw XML. 

The pattern of presenting a link to an RSS feed to the user that they can click on is *extremely common*. 

I don't want to appear hyperbolic here, but ending the capability of a user and a site owner to create an RSS feed that a user can click into and understand because it is visually rendered means we are fundamentally signing a death warrant for RSS feeds as an open technology. Inevitably we will have to alter our pages to link to entities running technologies that enclose and intermediate and disappear the open RSS feed, eventually one or a few of them will capture that process and people will find they have no choice but to link to their "feed" on that platform. 

This isn't a crazy out-there prediction, it's a pattern we've seen again and again. Arguably, it's how Twitter's popularity resulted in the death of RSS as a commonly-used standard the first time. So much of Twitter was just RSS feeds pushing into the platform's feed format. 

It is *particularly* wild to end this technology native-to-the-browser right as it is picking up again. As others and myself have noted, the injury of social media capture of the feed as a concept with the exodus from Twitter has opened up a new realm of experimentation around RSS, XML and XSLT.
